answer.label: Not George Carlin — actually Bob Moorehead
answer.authorDates: American pastor & author · senior pastor, Overlake Christian Church, 1970–1998
answer.sourceLine: The line opens “The Paradox of Our Age,” an essay by Dr. Bob Moorehead printed in his 1995 collection Words Aptly Spoken (Kirkland, WA: Overlake Christian Press), pp. 197–198. It reached the internet as an anonymous forward in 1998 and was pinned on Carlin, on the Dalai Lama, and on an unnamed Columbine student; Snopes rates the Carlin attribution False ↗ and Carlin denied it flatly in his lifetime.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Kirkland, WA: Overlake Christian Press, 1995 — pp. 197–198
Dr. Bob Moorehead, Overlake Christian Church

source.excerpt: We have taller buildings but shorter tempers; wider freeways but narrower viewpoints; we spend more but have less; we buy more but enjoy it less…
trail: 1995 — in print. Moorehead publishes Words Aptly Spoken, a collection of prayers, homilies and monologues from his sermons and radio broadcasts; Open Library records the Overlake Christian imprint and a December 1995 date ↗. “The Paradox of Our Age” sits at pp. 197–198.
May 1998 — it escapes. Jeff Dickson posts the essay to his Hacks-R-Us online forum, loosing it upon the internet, as Snopes puts it ↗. Dickson is not the author either.

1999 — the Carlin and Columbine forwards. Copies arrive headed “What a difference a sad event in someone’s life makes” with a note that Carlin’s wife had recently died; others credit an unnamed Columbine High School student. Wikiquote lists Carlin, a Columbine teen, the Dalai Lama, Anonymous and Octavian Paler among the hoax credits ↗.

Carlin’s own answer. He called the piece “a sappy load of shit” and posted a disclaimer on his website: “Nothing you see on the Internet is mine unless it came from one of my albums, books, HBO shows, or appeared on my website” ↗.
source.cutTag: the essay runs on for two printed pages
source.excerptNote: That is the wording of the printed essay, which Snopes reproduces beside the forwarded email ↗. Two differences are worth noting: in print the piece is titled “The Paradox of Our Age,” and the famous framing clause — “The paradox of our time in history is that” — belongs to the circulated version rather than to the book text.

source.rightsNote: Words Aptly Spoken was published in 1995, so the essay is well inside US copyright — nothing about its viral, unattributed circulation changes that. The excerpt above is quoted for identification and comment; rights rest with the author and Overlake Christian Press.

author.name: Bob Moorehead
author.heading: Who was Bob Moorehead?
author.metaLine: American pastor & author · senior pastor, Overlake Christian Church, 1970–1998
author.bio: Dr. Bob Moorehead led Overlake Christian Church in the Seattle suburbs from January 1970 until June 1998, building it from a small congregation into one of the region’s largest churches. Words Aptly Spoken (1995) gathered the prayers, homilies and monologues he used in sermons and on the radio — among them “The Paradox of Our Age,” which would go on to circulate worldwide under other people’s names. He resigned in 1998 amid allegations of sexual impropriety, and church elders later concluded he had violated the standards required of the office.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: Few texts have been recredited as often as this one. The essay travelled for years as an anonymous forward, and each wave of email attached whichever name made it land hardest.

items.scope: The whole essay, as “The Paradox of Our Time”
items.why: Forwards from 1999 carried the header “GEORGE CARLIN (His wife recently died…)” — a hook referring to Brenda Carlin, who died on 11 May 1997. Carlin rejected it outright, calling it “a sappy load of shit” and adding that it was “not only bad prose and poetry, it’s weak philosophy.” Wikiquote files it under Misattributed and credits Bob Moorehead ↗.

items.who: An unnamed Columbine High School student
items.why: In 1999, after the 20 April Columbine shootings, copies circulated under the header “A Columbine High School student wrote…” — a framing Snopes describes as infusing the essay with the significance folks thirsted for ↗.

items.who: The Dalai Lama (and, elsewhere, Octavian Paler or plain “Anonymous”)
items.why: The homiletic cadence reads as generically spiritual once the church context is stripped away, and the piece has been recirculated under all three credits. Wikiquote lists them among the web hoaxes ↗.
Dickson posted the essay to his Hacks-R-Us forum in May 1998, which is how it entered general circulation — but Snopes is explicit that the true author is not Dickson either ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Credit belongs to Dr. Bob Moorehead: “The Paradox of Our Age,” in Words Aptly Spoken (Kirkland, WA: Overlake Christian Press, 1995), pp. 197–198 — the citation Snopes prints in full ↗.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Carlin
lead: The essay was written for a pulpit, not a stage. Moorehead used it as a monologue in sermons and on the radio, and it sat quietly in a church-press paperback until Jeff Dickson posted it to an online forum in May 1998. From there it became one of the defining chain emails of the early web — a text with no author attached, forwarded into a vacuum that readers kept filling in.

Carlin was a natural guess and a terrible one. He was famous for scanning modern life and finding it absurd, so the shape of the piece fit; its earnest, consoling tone did not fit him at all. That mismatch is exactly what he objected to. The forward also came with a grief hook — a claim he had written it after his wife’s death — and Brenda Carlin had in fact died on 11 May 1997, which made the story feel checkable to people who never checked it.
detailsBody: Snopes first addressed the essay on 19 March 2001, in a fact check by Barbara Mikkelson, and rated the Carlin claim False. Its source list cites the Moorehead book directly, down to the page range.

The most instructive detail is the wording drift. The book text begins “We have taller buildings but shorter tempers”; the version everyone quotes begins “The paradox of our time in history is that…”. The famous opening clause was welded on somewhere in transmission, along with a retitling from “The Paradox of Our Age” to “The Paradox of Our Time.” The quote most people can recite is therefore a lightly edited forward of a printed sermon — which is part of why tracing it back to a 1995 church-press paperback took a fact checker to do.
context.pull: A text with no author attached, forwarded into a vacuum that readers kept filling in.
